```{r setup}
library(amorem)
```

## Why model invasions as relational events?

A non-native species establishing in a new country is a one-shot
directed event: source country `s` "invades" target country `r` at some
time `t`. Once `s` has reached `r`, the dyad `(s, r)` is removed from
the at-risk set — it cannot fire again. This is a **relational event
process** with a one-shot `risk = "remove"` rule.

Invasions unfold over centuries, so their rate can also follow the
climate: a covariate such as the El Niño/Southern Oscillation takes one
value per year for every dyad. This vignette builds an end-to-end
workflow in `amorem`:

1. Simulate five centuries of invasions driven by distance, an
   endogenous neighbour pressure, and the reconstructed ENSO index.
2. Draw a time-shifted case-control sample, which is what makes the
   ENSO effect estimable.
3. Recover all three drivers with `rem()`.

## Ingredients

We use the 56 × 56 US-state distance matrix shipped with `amorem` as a
stand-in for inter-country distances, and treat the states as the
country universe.

```{r data}
data("dist_matrix", package = "amorem")
states <- rownames(dist_matrix)

# Convert metres to log-units, scaled to a usable range.
dist_log <- log(dist_matrix / 1e5 + 1)
```

The global covariate is `enso_nino34`, the tree-ring reconstruction of the
winter Niño3.4 sea-surface temperature anomaly by Li et al. (2013), one
value per year from 1301 to 2005. We keep 1500–2005 and hold each winter's
value through the calendar year it opens:

```{r enso, fig.alt = "reconstructed Nino3.4 anomaly, 1500 to 2005"}
data("enso_nino34", package = "amorem")
enso <- enso_nino34[enso_nino34$year >= 1500, ]
g <- data.frame(time_start = enso$year, nino34 = enso$nino34)

plot(enso$year, enso$nino34, type = "l", col = "grey30",
     xlab = "year", ylab = "Niño3.4 anomaly (°C)",
     main = "Reconstructed ENSO index (Li et al. 2013)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey60")
```

## A simulated invasion record

The intensity of an invasion from `s` to `r` is

$$\lambda_{sr}(t) = Y_{sr}(t)\;\lambda_0\;\exp\!\bigl(f(d_{sr})
+ \beta_h\,h_{sr}(t) + \beta_g\,x(t)\bigr),$$

where $Y_{sr}(t)$ is the at-risk indicator (1 until `s` invades `r`,
0 thereafter), $d_{sr}$ is the log-distance with smooth effect
$f(d) = \sin(-d/1.5)$, $h_{sr}(t)$ is a neighbour pressure — here the
half-life-decayed count of past invasions in the reverse direction
(`reciprocity_exp_decay`, half-life 50 years) — and $x(t)$ is the ENSO
index. We set $\beta_h = 0.4$ and $\beta_g = 0.6$.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(4)
ev <- simulate_relational_events(
  n_events            = 600,
  senders             = states,
  receivers           = states,
  contribution_logits = sin(-dist_log / 1.5),
  baseline_rate       = 8e-4,
  start_time          = 1500,
  horizon             = 2005,
  allow_loops         = FALSE,
  endogenous_stats    = "reciprocity_exp_decay",
  endogenous_effects  = c(reciprocity_exp_decay = 0.4),
  half_life           = 50,
  global_covariates   = g,
  global_effects      = c(nino34 = 0.6),
  risk                = "remove"
)
ev <- ev[, c("sender", "receiver", "time")]
nrow(ev)
range(ev$time)
```

`risk = "remove"` guarantees the realized dyads are all distinct:

```{r unique-check}
any(duplicated(paste(ev$sender, ev$receiver)))
```

## Why ordinary case-control sampling cannot see ENSO

Standard nested case-control sampling gives each control its event's
time. ENSO then takes the same value for the event and its control, so
its event-minus-control difference is zero in every stratum and the
effect drops out of the partial likelihood:

```{r no-shift}
cc0 <- sample_non_events(ev, mode = "one", risk = "remove", seed = 1)
cc0$nino34 <- g$nino34[findInterval(cc0$time, g$time_start)]
w0 <- widen_case_control(cc0, covariates = "nino34")
all(w0$d_nino34 == 0)
```

## Time-shifted sampling

Lembo, Juozaitienė, Vinciotti & Wit (2025) sample the controls from a
time-shifted copy of the process instead. Every dyad draws one shift
$h_{sr}$; event $k$ moves to $t_k + h_{s_k r_k}$, and its control is
drawn among the dyads whose back-shifted time
$t^* = t_k + h_{s_k r_k} - h_{s^* r^*}$ lies in the observation window.
The control is evaluated at its own time $t^*$, where the ENSO index
takes a different value. With `risk = "remove"`, a dyad that has
already fired before $t^*$ is not a valid control.

```{r shift}
cc <- sample_non_events(ev, mode = "one", risk = "remove", seed = 1,
                        shift = "exponential", window = c(1500, 2005))
attr(cc, "shift")$mean            # mean shift, in years
length(attr(cc, "shift")$uninformative)
```

Every covariate of a control is then evaluated at its own time. The
neighbour pressure comes from the real invasions before $t^*$
(`history_log`), distance is static, and ENSO is read at each row's
year:

```{r covariates}
cc <- endogenous_features(cc, stats = "reciprocity_exp_decay",
                          half_life = 50, history_log = ev)
cc$dist   <- dist_log[cbind(match(cc$sender, states),
                            match(cc$receiver, states))]
cc$nino34 <- g$nino34[findInterval(cc$time, g$time_start)]

w <- widen_case_control(cc, covariates = c("dist", "reciprocity_exp_decay",
                                           "nino34", "time"))
summary(w$d_nino34)
```

## Recovering the drivers

`rem()` fits the degenerate logistic additive model on the wide
case–control table. `nl(dist)` is the smooth distance effect,
contributing $f(d_{ev}) - f(d_{nv})$; the other two terms are linear.

```{r recovery}
fit <- rem(~ nl(dist) + reciprocity_exp_decay + nino34,
           data = w, method = "gam")
est <- summary(fit)$p.table[, c("Estimate", "Std. Error")]
round(est, 3)
```

```{r recovery-numbers, include = FALSE}
b  <- est[, "Estimate"]
se <- est[, "Std. Error"]
z  <- (b - c(0.4, 0.6)) / se
```

The ENSO coefficient is `r sprintf("%.2f", b[["nino34"]])` (standard error
`r sprintf("%.2f", se[["nino34"]])`) against the true 0.6. The neighbour
pressure, `r sprintf("%.2f", b[["reciprocity_exp_decay"]])` against the true 0.4,
has a standard error of `r sprintf("%.2f", se[["reciprocity_exp_decay"]])`,
`r sprintf("%.0f", se[["reciprocity_exp_decay"]] / se[["nino34"]])` times larger:
few invasions are preceded by one in the opposite direction, so the data
hold little information about it. The two estimates lie
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(z[["nino34"]]))` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(z[["reciprocity_exp_decay"]]))` standard errors from their
true values. The smooth recovers the shape of the distance effect, up to
the additive constant that cancels in event-minus-control differences:

```{r distance-smooth, fig.alt = "recovered smooth distance effect against the true curve"}
plot(fit, select = 1, shade = TRUE, rug = FALSE,
     xlab = "log-distance", ylab = "f(log-distance)",
     main = "Distance effect: estimate and truth")
d_grid <- seq(min(dist_log[dist_log > 0]), max(dist_log), length.out = 200)
f_true <- sin(-d_grid / 1.5)
lines(d_grid, f_true - mean(f_true), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("estimate", "truth (centred)"),
       col = c("black", "firebrick"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

## Where to go from here

- Real data: replace `dist_matrix` with a country-by-country distance
  table and the simulated log with a curated invasion record of first
  establishments.
- Baseline trend: on real data the background rate changes over the
  centuries (trade, shipping, survey effort). It is a global effect too,
  and enters as `nl(time)` on the same shifted design.
- Timing: `shift_scale` sets the mean shift as a multiple of the average
  event time. Larger shifts carry more information about ENSO but leave
  more events with no valid control (`attr(cc, "shift")$uninformative`).
- For large state spaces or high invasion rates, switch to the
  approximate `method = "tau_leap"` simulator with a small `tau`; the
  `risk = "remove"` rule is honoured under both algorithms.

## References

Li J, Xie S-P, Cook ER, et al. (2013). El Niño modulations over the past
seven centuries. *Nature Climate Change* 3, 822–826.
<https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate1936>

Lembo M, Juozaitienė R, Vinciotti V, Wit EC (2025). Relational event
models with global covariates: an application to bike sharing. *Journal
of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C*.
<https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssc/qlaf058>
